A reader cannot see why the fourth power arises (rather than the \(\Delta^2\) familiar from uncompressed testing), which is precisely the informational content of the distance reduction. Positioning omits the one comparison a referee will demand: how a_n=(log n/n)^{1/4} relates to the uncompressed uniform benchmark. For a bivariate design with smoothness q, the standard sup-norm rate is (log n/n)^{q/(2q+2)}, which equals a_n exactly at q=1 and is strictly faster for q>=2; likewise the signed matched rate is order-free in p even though the class carries C^{p+1} regressions. Add a paragraph to the Introduction (after the packing heuristic) and to Related Literature stating: compression is non-binding at q=1 and binding for q>=2, and the signed frontier is flat in p, so additional smoothness or polynomial order buys constants rather than exponent. Without this the reader cannot tell what the compression actually costs.

The mechanism behind the fourth-order information calculation is asserted, never explained. The Introduction writes "Unsigned distance compression leaves each coordinate with information of order n\Delta^4" and the packing proof states a one-point KL bound C_KL\delta_n^4, but nowhere is it said that radial invariance (equality of the distance marginals after a bit flip) annihilates the first- and second-order terms so that the leading KL contribution is quartic. Insert two sentences after the displayed calibration n\Delta^4 \asymp \log M in the Main Results discussion of \cref{obj:thm:cty-same-class-log-converse} explaining that the flip preserves the unsigned distance law exactly, so the divergence is driven by a fourth-order remainder; this is the single idea on which both converses rest.

Rewrite that paragraph so the packing plus overlap product yields the point-indexed converse first and the common-map converse follows by the class inclusion, and move \cref{obj:lem:common-map-strict-in-point-indexed} ahead of the packing discussion. The compression/'information barrier' reading of the unsigned converse is asserted without the uncompressed benchmark (Introduction, 'Thus the logarithmic lower bound is tied to the unsigned distance information set itself...'; Discussion ¶1, 'These conclusions identify an information barrier created by unsigned distance compression'). For Hölder-q regression on a two-dimensional design, the classical uniform sup-norm rate is (log n/n)^{q/(2q+2)}, which equals a_n exactly at q=1; so at q=1 the theorem is consistent with no loss at all from distance compression, and the bound is informative about compression only for q≥2. Fix: display the uncompressed benchmark rate with a citation (Stone 1982 / Tsybakov 2009), state the comparison explicitly, and rephrase the claim as 'the unsigned lower bound does not improve with q' rather than as an identified barrier.

The central mechanism of both constructions — why the coordinatewise Kullback--Leibler budget is of order Δ^4 rather than the Δ^2 a reader expects for a mean shift of size Δ — is never explained in prose. The Introduction's calculation after Theorem obj:thm:cty-same-class-log-converse simply writes 'Unsigned distance compression leaves each coordinate with information of order nΔ^4' and calls it 'the fourth-order distance-compression information calculation', and Appendix C reproduces the same Δ^4/w^2 bound for the signed hypercube where no angular information is discarded. Fix: add a short paragraph (after the packing calculation in Section 4, referenced again before Lemma obj:lem:cty-a1-a2-rectangle-angular-hypercube-all-orders) explaining that the perturbations are built to leave the radial (resp. signed-distance) marginal invariant — as recorded in the radial-invariance and common-signed-marginal clauses — so the first-order divergence term cancels and a fourth-order remainder governs the budget in both experiments.

The matched signed-distance rate is independent of the polynomial order p, which contradicts the reader's expectation from the local-polynomial RD literature that a degree-p fit has bias O(h^{p+1}); the reason is that the only bias input assumed is first order (obj:synth_39 and the second bullet of obj:synth_139 bound BiasRatio, i.e. bias of order h, uniformly over the class), yet the paper only remarks that 'the polynomial order p likewise affects constants and regularity thresholds while the displayed rate normalization remains a_n' (Section 4, after Theorem obj:thm:cty-same-class-log-converse). Fix: add explicit discussion where obj:synth_39 is introduced explaining why the class-uniform bias along the whole interface is only first order (interface curvature and two-sided window geometry, not the smoothness of the arm regressions), and state plainly in the Discussion that the frontier therefore makes no claim that higher p improves the uniform rate.

The relationship between what Appendix B proves and what obj:synth_139 assumes is left for the reader to reconstruct, which obscures how much of the upper bound is imported. Lemma obj:lem:cty-winsorized-score-maximal-bound already establishes an expected outer maximal bound for the winsorized score, uniform over the class, from the VC certificate of Lemma obj:lem:euclidean-balls-vc; the assumed input nonetheless posits the same-shaped bound for the raw (unwinsorized) score with the heavy-tail exponent n^{(1+ν)/(2+ν)}, and also assumes the Gram deviation bound even though the Gram entries have a bounded envelope and the same ball class. Fix: add a paragraph at the end of Appendix B stating exactly which pieces of the assumed input remain open (raw-score centering with the moment-envelope exponent; the Gram supremum) and why the proved lemma plus the winsorization bias bound do not close them, and repeat that scope sentence once in the Discussion.

The assumption inventory of obj:def:cty-a1-a2-class contains a clause the paper itself proves and several thresholds it never interprets. The 'Metric, kernel, and VC bound' bullet assumes the ball class has VC index at most four, which is precisely the content of Lemma obj:lem:euclidean-balls-vc for closed Euclidean balls in the plane; carrying it as a class hypothesis inflates the apparent assumption burden. Separately, the population Gram lower bound, small-bandwidth arm mass, distance-slice density, and the threshold L_0(p) ≥ 48 are stated with no verifying example beyond the corner check for the fixed rectangle. Fix: delete the VC clause from the definition and record it as a remark backed by the lemma; and add one worked example (a smooth convex interface with positive reach inside the rectangle) verifying the Gram and arm-mass thresholds, plus a sentence noting that L ≥ L_0(p) enlarges the law class rather than restricting the data-generating process.

L ≥ L_0' and '(Risk definition.)' as bullets under 'there exists a real number L_0 such that', garbling the quantifier structure over free variables ν and L, and its conclusion opens with the vacuous identity liminf a_n^{-1}R = liminf R/a_n (likewise in the two unsigned theorems); restate hypotheses before the existential and delete the identity. The two constructions that carry the entire lower-bound program — \cref{obj:lem:cty-support-boundary-angular-packing} and \cref{obj:lem:cty-a1-a2-rectangle-angular-hypercube-all-orders} — have proofs that delegate to unnamed objects ("the assembly certificate", "the constructor data for order p", "the hard-hypercube assembly", "the population-Gram certificate", the undefined constant D_q and C_KL). The fourth-order information calibration is asserted rather than explained, and it is the crux of both results. In \cref{sec:main-results} the sentence "Unsigned distance compression leaves each coordinate with information of order n\Delta^4" gives no reason why a perturbation of height Delta on a cell of area w^2 contributes per-observation KL of order Delta^4/w^2 rather than the naive Delta^2, and the same Delta^4/w^2 bound reappears in \cref{obj:lem:cty-a1-a2-rectangle-angular-hypercube-all-orders} where the rule additionally knows the geometry and the treatment side. Fix: add a short subsection deriving the cancellation (the perturbation is arranged to have vanishing conditional mean and vanishing first-order term on each distance slice, so only a quartic remainder survives the radial/signed marginal), and state explicitly why side and geometry knowledge does not defeat it.

The three analytic inputs are labelled "the CTY distance-identification, uniform first-order bias, and expected maximal inputs" in the abstract, introduction, and \cref{obj:synth_139}, which reads as though \citet{CattaneoTitiunikYu2026Distance} supply them, while \cref{sec:related-literature} concedes that CTY provide "sequence-scoped bias expansions, and probability-order stochastic control". The assumed versions are uniform over P in the displayed class and stated in outer expectation, which is strictly stronger. Fix: add a remark immediately after \cref{obj:synth_139} stating precisely how each input strengthens the cited results, noting that \cref{obj:lem:cty-winsorized-score-maximal-bound} already delivers the winsorized-score half and naming exactly what remains (raw-score de-winsorization with the n^{(1+nu)/(2+nu)} heavy-tail term, and the Gram bound), and stating that no member law of P_12(p,nu,L) is exhibited for which AI is verified.

The matched rate a_n is the same for every polynomial order p, which will read to an econometrics audience as either an error or a deep phenomenon, and the paper does neither. The reason is that the assumed bias input caps the population approximation error at order h rather than h^{p+1}, so a degree-p fit under C^{p+1} smoothness buys nothing in rate. Fix: add a remark after \cref{obj:prop:cty-a1-a2-winsorized-expected-outer-upper} explaining why the signed-distance reduction limits the achievable bias order to the first, contrast a_n with the uniform boundary rates one would obtain from a bivariate local-polynomial fit at smoothness p+1, and say plainly that the matched frontier for large p is a statement about the distance-reduced experiment rather than about the underlying smoothness class.

Formalization artifacts and undefined notation appear in reader-facing statements: \operatorname{ofReal}(c) in the proof of \cref{obj:thm:cty-a1-a2-winsorized-matched-frontier}, the Lean identifiers CtyDistanceIdentification, CtyUniformFirstOrderBias, CtyExpectedLocalPolynomialMaximalBounds inside \cref{obj:synth_139}, the never-defined \widehat m_{t,x}(h_n), m_{t,P,x}(h_n) in the third bullet of that same theorem, the never-defined packing loss \ell_{n,P}^{\mathrm{pack}} in the converse proof, and bullet lists that mix genuine hypotheses with definitions and free-parameter restrictions inside an existential (\cref{obj:thm:cty-a1-a2-point-indexed-log-converse-all-orders} literally asserts "there exists L_0 such that: (Moment exponent) nu >= 2"). The trivially true normalization identities liminf (n/log n)^{1/4}R = liminf R/a_n in all three theorems are also noise. Fix: restate the three theorems in ordinary quantifier prose, delete the normalization identities, define or remove the orphan symbols, and move Lean names into \cref{sec:verification-note} together with a repository URL, commit hash, toolchain version, and a table mapping each anchored statement to its Lean declaration (the appendix currently claims a checked formal layer with no artifact a reader can obtain).

The "shared scale" framing overstates what is established, because the unsigned side has only a lower bound. The abstract's "unsigned distance observations cannot uniformly recover independently varying boundary values at this scale", the introduction's "The common normalization a_n therefore records a shared logarithmic uniform-risk scale across the two formal experiments", and the abstract's negation-shaped sentence together suggest a rate comparison that the results do not support: a_n may be far from the unsigned minimax rate, and the agreement is mechanical, arising because both constructions use the same fourth-order KL calibration. Fix: recast these three sentences affirmatively and precisely — state that both experiments admit hard families calibrated by the same fourth-order compressed-information budget, that the signed experiment is pinned two-sidedly under AI, and that the unsigned statement is a converse for the displayed class — and add one sentence in \cref{sec:discussion} naming the best unsigned upper bound the authors can currently assert.

Abstract and introduction: phrases like “compact nonparametric law class” may overstate compactness of the law class itself; revise to “compact-support nonparametric law class” unless formal compactness is actually established.

The three analytic inputs collected as AI_{p,nu,L} (\cref{obj:synth_139}) are attributed to the CTY framework, but they are stated in a strictly stronger form than the Related Literature paragraph itself describes CTY as delivering: that paragraph says CTY provides "sequence-scoped bias expansions, and probability-order stochastic control," whereas the third bullet of AI assumes *expected outer* maximal bounds holding *uniformly over every P in P_12(p,nu,L)* along every admissible bandwidth sequence. The rate a_n=(log n/n)^{1/4} is claimed to be the matched signed-distance rate for *every* fixed polynomial order p, yet the only bias control assumed is first order (BiasRatio_{p,nu',L}(h_n) = O(1), i.e. bias of order h) even though \cref{obj:def:cty-a1-a2-class} imposes C^{p+1} potential-outcome regressions. A reader who balances an h^{p+1} bias against the stochastic scale {log(h^{-1})/(nh^2)}^{1/2} obtains a rate faster than a_n for p>=1, which appears to contradict \cref{obj:thm:cty-a1-a2-point-indexed-log-converse-all-orders}. Fix: insert a paragraph after \cref{obj:prop:cty-a1-a2-winsorized-expected-outer-upper} explaining why the signed-distance reduction caps the achievable bias order at h regardless of p (presumably because the induced one-dimensional regression u -> theta_t(u) inherits only first-order smoothness from curved distance level sets), and state affirmatively in Section \ref{sec:main-results} that higher polynomial order changes constants and thresholds but not the exponent, with the reason.

The heuristic calibration in Section \ref{sec:main-results} ("Unsigned distance compression leaves each coordinate with information of order n\Delta^4") is the load-bearing step of the whole paper's exponent, and it is asserted rather than explained; \cref{obj:lem:cty-support-boundary-angular-packing} likewise records the KL bound alpha log M_n with the mechanism buried in a one-line reference to a "one-point radial KL constant" and "C_KL delta_n^4". Fix: add three or four sentences after the display giving the source of the fourth power (the first-order effect of the bump cancels in the radial marginal at the query point, leaving a second-order perturbation whose chi-square/KL is quadratic in it), and state where the Holder order q enters and why it does not touch the exponent.

The unsigned experiment involves no treatment assignment, no assignment regions, and no discontinuity: the target is the boundary regression curve mu_P on bd(X_P) under the class of \cref{obj:def:cty-nonparametric-class}. Calling it a "boundary regression discontinuity experiment" in the first sentence of the abstract, and framing the paper's title around boundary regression, overstates the RD content of half the results. Fix: in the abstract and the opening of Section \ref{sec:unsigned-setup}, describe the unsigned problem affirmatively as uniform boundary-curve regression under distance compression, and reserve RD language for the signed known-geometry experiment where potential outcomes and a treatment interface are actually present.

The paper repeatedly presents the shared normalization a_n as an agreement across the two experiments (abstract final sentences; Introduction penultimate paragraph; Section \ref{sec:discussion} third paragraph), but the two statements are of different types: an unmatched lower bound for mu_P over P_NP(L,q), and a conditional two-sided rate for tau_P over P_12(p,nu,L). Because no unsigned upper bound is established, the coincidence of lower scales cannot support any conclusion about the relative difficulty of unsigned versus signed observation. Fix: add one explicit sentence in Section \ref{sec:discussion} stating what the coincidence does and does not license (it records two separately established lower scales on a common normalization; ranking the two information sets would require a matching unsigned upper bound), so the reader does not infer that sign and angle information are costless.

Two definitional/notational defects should be repaired.
